We've seen multiple examples of why granting Meta's Muse app Full Disk Access on Mac is an exceptionally bad idea, and another major privacy issue has just been exposed. Muse has been found to be analyzing your communications with everyone in your life on an hourly basis.

It's reasonable for Apple to express concern about this development, and the company said in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls for the Full Disk Access feature that has been fueling this problem.

Meta's Muse app makes the situation urgent

Meta recently launched its Muse personal AI agent assistant for iPhone and Mac. Despite the fact that granting a Meta app full access to all your Apple devices is clearly not something to be encouraged, the app quickly surged to the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, things quickly started going badly wrong, and they haven't improved since — *Wired* reports that security researcher Karan Joshi found that Meta had instructed Muse to harvest all the data necessary to build a complete map of all your relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to give it the ability to "build profile pages for every person in the user's life." This hourly process involves collecting data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "collaborators," and people you "follow," with instructions stating: "Where they live, what they do for work, what they talk about often (moving, joint savings goals)." It also states that the model can record "important dates" such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's experiences might include background details like "a March trip, a resolved argument, last week's milestone."

Apple tightens Full Disk Access

You might think the prompt requesting Full Disk Access on a Mac is self-explanatory, but that clearly isn't the case. Even tech-savvy users have granted this blanket permission without realizing just how dangerous this step is.

Apple says the feature was originally designed for backup apps, but developers have since used it for a much wider range of purposes, including AI assistants. The company said it intends to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when granting this permission.

What Apple must and must not do

Apple says this step is "critical," and I completely agree. When existing permission requests clearly fail to adequately convey the gravity of granting this access, Apple must ensure users truly understand what they're allowing.

I'd very much like to see clearer, more explicit wording advising people not to do this unless they're sure they understand the consequences. Something along these lines:

Basically, stronger language cannot be too strong. I'd also welcome a one-time confirmation for apps that have already been granted this permission.

Peter — most upvoted comment

While I find it a bit annoying that Apple periodically asks me to confirm whether I still want to grant an app location access, I do appreciate this design. There was one time when I realized I no longer wanted a particular app to have that level of access. It also reminds me to periodically think about which apps might be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat the mistake it made with screen recording on macOS Sequoia. That approach is itself just as dangerous, and issuing strong warnings is certainly appropriate, but what Apple did at the time was force us to confirm these permissions every week and every time we restarted the computer.

This move was widely criticized as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing a "subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, Apple's occasional repeated permission requests on iPhone have already gone too far. For example, I've granted Citymapper access to my location so it can provide continuous background navigation; Apple, I really don't need you asking me again whether I still want to do this.

There should absolutely be the strongest possible warning for granting Full Disk Access, but if someone chooses to do so, macOS must respect their decision. Thank you, but no weekly or other periodic mandatory confirmations.
